turns.text: Explain how the TCP three-way handshake works.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Two computers want to talk reliably, so TCP opens a connection first. Here are the client on the left and the server on the right, each with its own timeline running down.
Step one: the client sends a SYN, a synchronise packet, carrying its initial sequence number, say x. That means: I'd like to open a connection, and my data will start numbering from x.

Step two: the server replies with SYN and ACK together. It acknowledges x with x plus one, and offers its own starting number, y. So it confirms it heard the client and asks for a connection of its own.

draw.label: SYN + ACK, seq = y, ack = x + 1

beats.say: Step three: the client answers with ACK, acknowledging y with y plus one. Now both sides have sent and confirmed their sequence numbers, so the connection is established.

draw.text: Connection established - data can flow both ways

beats.say: Why not two steps? Because each side needs to prove both that it can send and that it can receive. Three messages confirm that in both directions, and the random starting numbers stop old, delayed packets from being mistaken for new data.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply:
Sure — think of it as a phone call where both sides say "hello" and get a "hello back."

The client asks to connect with a SYN. The server answers with a SYN-ACK, saying "got it, and here's mine." Then the client sends an ACK saying "got yours too." Three messages, and both directions are confirmed.

beats.say: Here's the plain version, in the empty space above.

draw.text: Simple version: like saying hello, hello back, got it

beats.say: Client says: can we talk? That's the SYN.
Server says: yes, can you hear me too? That's the SYN-ACK.
Client says: yes I can. That's the ACK, and now both sides can talk.

turns.text: What happens if the SYN-ACK gets lost?
turns.reply:
Good question — it's a timeout, not a failure.

turns.text: How does OAuth login with Google work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

lesson.title: How OAuth login with Google works

beats.say: OAuth login with Google lets a website log you in without ever seeing your password. Four parties are involved: your browser, the app you're signing into, Google, and Google's servers behind the scenes.
First you click Sign in with Google. The app redirects your browser to Google with its client ID, the scopes it wants, and a redirect URI where Google should send you back.
Google shows its own consent screen, and you sign in and approve. The important part: you type your password into Google, never into the app.
Google sends your browser back to the app's redirect URI with a short-lived one-time authorization code in the URL. The code is not an access token yet.

The browser hands that code to the app's server, which exchanges it with Google over a private back channel, including its client secret. Google checks the code and returns an ID token and an access token.

The app verifies the ID token's signature and claims, reads your email and name, and creates its own session cookie. From then on you're simply logged in, and the tokens can be refreshed or revoked later.

draw.text: verify signature + claims, then log in

turns.text: More detail on the access token.

beats.say: The access token is what the app uses to actually call Google's APIs on your behalf — like reading your profile or calendar. Notice its path: it goes from Google's token endpoint straight to your app's server and stays there, locked to Google's servers and never handed to the browser.

draw.text: verify signature + claims, then log in

beats.say: A few properties matter. It is opaque, usually a random string rather than something you can read — unlike the ID token, which is a JWT about who you are. It is short-lived, often about an hour, and its scope limits exactly which APIs it can touch.

draw.text: opaque string, not a JWT about you

beats.say: When it expires, the refresh token comes in: the server quietly exchanges it for a fresh access token, so you don't sign in again. Logging out, or revoking access in your Google account, kills the whole chain.

turns.text: What happens when I type a website name and DNS looks it up?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out for you.

lesson.title: How DNS Resolves a Website Name

beats.say: When you type a name like example.com, your computer can't use it as-is. It needs an IP address. That lookup job is called DNS resolution.

draw.text: Typing a name → finding its IP address

beats.say: First the resolver checks its own cache. If someone asked recently and the answer hasn't expired, it replies instantly and the lookup is over.
If not cached, it starts at the root servers, which point it to the right top-level domain, like dot com. Each answer is a pointer to the next place to ask.
The TLD servers point to the site's authoritative name server. That one holds the real record and finally hands back the IP address.
The resolver caches that answer, returns it to your computer, and your browser opens the connection using the IP address instead of the name.

draw.text: Cached, returned, browser connects to the IP

turns.text: Where does caching happen?

beats.say: The cache you saw isn't just one thing. Your browser, your operating system, and the resolver each keep their own copies.
When you look something up, your computer checks the browser first, then the OS, then asks the resolver. Only a miss at every level means a real trip to the root.
How long each copy lives is set by a TTL, a time-to-live written into the record itself. Once it expires, the entry is thrown away and looked up fresh.

draw.text: Each record carries a TTL that sets how long a cached copy stays valid

turns.text: How does HTTPS keep my connection secure?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

lesson.title: How HTTPS Keeps Your Connection Secure

beats.say: HTTPS is just HTTP with a TLS layer wrapped around it. The point is three things: nobody can read your traffic, nobody can change it in transit, and you're actually talking to the real site.
First, the handshake. The server proves who it is with a certificate signed by a trusted authority, so an impostor can't sit in the middle pretending to be your bank.
Then they agree on a shared secret key without ever sending it in the clear. That's the clever bit: each side mixes in a private value, and only the two of them can work out the same result.
From then on, everything you send is scrambled with that key, and every message carries a check value called a MAC. If anyone tampers with even one byte, the check fails and the connection dies.
So the padlock means three guarantees: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication of the server. Your password and card number stay private, and nobody swaps the page under you.

turns.text: More detail on the certificate check.

lesson.title: How HTTPS Keeps Your Connection Secure

beats.say: The certificate is a signed statement that says: this public key belongs to this exact domain name. Your browser trusts the signature because it already has the issuer's root key built in.

draw.text: cert = domain name + public key + expiry, signed by issuer

beats.say: The check is a chain. The server sends its certificate plus the intermediate certificates in between, and the browser walks that chain up until it reaches a root it already trusts.

It then checks four things: the signature verifies at every link, the names match the site you typed, the certificate hasn't expired, and it isn't on a revocation list. Any failure and you get a full-page warning.

draw.text: checks: signature ✓ name ✓ dates ✓ not revoked ✓

beats.say: The keys matter too. Certificates use slow asymmetric crypto only to agree on that shared key; after that, everything switches to fast symmetric encryption.

draw.text: asymmetric for the handshake, symmetric for the bulk data

beats.say: One honest caveat: it proves you're talking to whoever controls that domain, not that the company is trustworthy. A phishing site can have a perfectly valid certificate.

draw.text: valid cert = right domain, not necessarily honest site

turns.text: Explain the OSI model layers.
turns.reply: Sure, let me sketch the OSI model out for you.

beats.say: The OSI model splits network communication into seven stacked layers, each one handing work to the layer below it.
The top three layers are about the application itself. Layer 7 is what you actually use — HTTP, email, DNS.
Layer 4, transport, is the traffic cop — it breaks data into segments, adds port numbers, and picks TCP for reliability or UDP for speed.
Layer 3, network, handles logical addressing and routing. This is where IP addresses live and routers make their decisions.
Layer 2, data link, moves frames between devices on the same local network using MAC addresses, framing and error checking.
Layer 1, physical, is the raw stuff — cables, radio, voltage and bits on the wire. Each layer on one machine talks to its twin on the other.

turns.text: Which layer does a router work at?

beats.say: A router works at layer 3, the network layer, because that's where IP addresses live.

draw.text: Reads the IP address on each packet

beats.say: It reads the destination IP and forwards the packet toward the next hop, connecting different networks together.

draw.text: Joins separate networks, hop by hop

beats.say: Handy comparison: a switch is layer 2 and uses MAC addresses, while a router is layer 3 and uses IP addresses.

draw.text: Switch = L2, MACs   |   Router = L3, IPs

turns.text: Give me an example of a packet going down the layers.
turns.reply: Let me trace one packet down the stack.

lesson.title: A Packet Going Down the Layers

beats.say: Say you open a webpage. At layer 7 you just type a request — HTTP asks for the page.
Layer 4 chops it into segments and stamps port numbers on them, with TCP tracking reliability.
Layer 3 wraps each segment in a packet with source and destination IP addresses.
Layer 2 frames it with MAC addresses for the next device, plus a checksum to catch errors.
Layer 1 turns it all into electrical signals or light and puts it on the cable. On the far side, every layer unwraps its header in reverse.

turns.text: How does a load balancer spread traffic across servers?
turns.reply: I'll sketch this out for you.

lesson.title: How a Load Balancer Spreads Traffic

beats.say: Clients send every request to one address, the load balancer, which acts as the front door.

draw.text: How a load balancer spreads traffic

beats.say: Behind it sit several identical servers. They can be added or removed without clients noticing.
The simplest method is round robin: request one to server one, request two to server two, and so on in a loop.
Least connections instead sends each new request to whichever server currently has the fewest active ones, which handles slow requests better.

draw.text: Least connections: fewest busy server wins

beats.say: A health check pings each server, and if one stops answering the balancer quietly stops sending it traffic.
Some also keep a session sticky, so a returning user lands on the same server that holds their data.

draw.text: Sticky sessions: same user, same server

turns.text: What happens when one server goes down?
turns.reply: I'll add that to the board.

beats.say: Say server three crashes. Its health check suddenly fails, so the balancer marks it unhealthy.
From then on it takes server three out of the rotation entirely, so no new requests are sent there.
Its share just gets divided among the healthy servers, so each of them picks up a bit more load.
Clients never notice: their requests keep working, they're just served by a different machine.
If that server recovers, it passes the health check again and rejoins the pool for new traffic.

turns.text: How does a CDN make websites faster?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out for you.

lesson.title: How a CDN Speeds Up Websites

beats.say: A CDN, or content delivery network, is a set of servers spread all over the world that keep copies of a website's files close to the people viewing it.

draw.text: How a CDN makes sites faster

beats.say: Without a CDN, every visitor's request travels all the way to one origin server, which might be an ocean away. That long round trip is pure waiting time.

draw.text: One origin server = high latency for distant users

beats.say: With a CDN, the first request pulls a copy of the page into a nearby edge server, which caches it. Everyone else nearby is then served locally.

Distance is the big win, but there are two more. Traffic is spread across many machines, so one server isn't overwhelmed, and files are served over already-warm connections, cutting handshake overhead.

draw.text: 1. Low latency: data travels a shorter distance
2. Load spreading: no single server bottleneck
3. Fewer round trips: reused, optimised connections

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Let me simplify it on the board.

lesson.title: How a CDN Speeds Up Websites

beats.say: Here's the simple version. Think of one big server as one shop in one city.
If you live far from that shop, every trip is a long one, and you just wait.

draw.text: You wait, because it's far away.

beats.say: A CDN is like opening copy shops in lots of cities. Each one keeps the same goods on hand.
Now you walk to the shop on your street instead. Short trip, fast answer. That's the whole idea.

draw.text: You're served from the nearest copy, so pages load fast.

turns.text: How is a WebSocket different from normal HTTP requests?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: Both start the same way, with a normal HTTP request, but they end up very differently.
Plain HTTP is one-shot: the client asks, the server answers, and the connection is basically done. Every new piece of data needs a brand new request.
Each of those requests carries headers like cookies and user-agent, over and over. That overhead adds up when you need updates many times a second.
A WebSocket begins as one HTTP request with an Upgrade header. If the server agrees, that same connection turns into a WebSocket instead of closing.

draw.text: one handshake, then the connection stays open

beats.say: After that handshake the connection stays open, and both sides can send messages whenever they like, without asking permission first. That's called full duplex.
So the short version: HTTP is request-reply, stateless, and starts fresh each time. A WebSocket is one long-lived, two-way pipe, which is why chat, live scores and collaborative editors use it.

draw.text:
HTTP: ask → answer → done
WebSocket: open once, talk both ways

turns.text: Show me the upgrade step in more detail.

beats.say: Let's zoom into that purple Upgrade arrow. The client sends an ordinary GET request, but with two special headers: Upgrade: websocket and a Connection: upgrade header.
It also sends Sec-WebSocket-Key, a random base64 value, and a Sec-WebSocket-Version of 13. Notice there's no request body: this is not a normal data request.

draw.text:
Sec-WebSocket-Key: random
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
no request body

beats.say: The server answers with 101 Switching Protocols, plus a Sec-WebSocket-Accept value it computes by hashing the client's key with a fixed GUID. That proves both sides really speak WebSocket.
From this moment there is no more HTTP on this socket. The very same TCP connection is now framed as WebSocket messages, which is why no new connection or headers are needed.

draw.text: same TCP socket — HTTP ends here, WebSocket begins

beats.say: If the server ignores the headers and just returns a normal 200 response, there's no handshake and the client falls back to HTTP. Also note wss uses TLS exactly like https does.

draw.text:
server says 200 → no upgrade, plain HTTP
authentication still applies at handshake time

turns.text: How does React decide what to re-render?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out.

lesson.title: How React decides what to re-render

beats.say: React re-renders when state or props change, and it does that top-down, from the component that changed.

draw.text: How React decides what to re-render

beats.say: Each render produces a new tree of elements, and React compares it to the previous tree. This diffing is the reconciliation step.
Same type and same position means React keeps the DOM node and just updates changed attributes and text. That's the cheap path.

draw.label: Same type + key: update in place

beats.say: Different type, or a changed key, means React unmounts the old subtree and mounts a fresh one, so state inside it is thrown away.
The trick is that a parent re-rendering will call its children's render functions too, even if their props are unchanged, unless you stop it.
That is what memo, PureComponent and callbacks like useMemo and useCallback are for: they let React skip a subtree when inputs are shallow-equal.
Finally, after reconciliation React commits only the real DOM changes, then runs effects and layout effects. So render is cheap work you can interrupt, and commit is the part that touches the screen.

turns.text: More detail on the virtual DOM diff.

lesson.title: How React decides what to re-render

beats.say: The diff is not a general tree comparison. React walks both trees at the same time and only looks at the same position, so it stays linear instead of quadratic.
It compares element type first, then key if there's a list. Same type means it keeps the DOM node and recurses into the children, patching only attributes that actually changed.
Different type means a rebuild: the old node and its whole subtree go away, state included. React doesn't try to be clever about it.
For lists, keys are the whole game. Without keys React matches siblings by index, so inserting at the top shifts everything and can destroy state in items that didn't really change.
Fragments, arrays and conditional children all follow those same rules: a falsy child is just skipped, and a keyed child that reappears later is a new mount.
One more thing worth knowing: the render pass can be paused or thrown away, so never mutate state or DOM during render. Only the commit phase is guaranteed to land.

turns.text: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: JavaScript runs on one thread, so it can only do one thing at a time. Here's the main piece: the call stack, where your functions actually execute, plus the queues waiting for their turn.

draw.text: runs one function at a time

beats.say: When you call a function it gets pushed onto the stack, and it pops off when it returns. If the stack is busy, nothing else can run — that's why a long loop freezes the page.
Async work like timers or network calls gets handed off to the browser. When it's done, the callback doesn't run immediately — it's parked in a queue instead.
Now the magic bit. Whenever the stack is empty, the loop drains the entire microtask queue first, one microtask after another, before touching anything else.
Only when the microtasks are fully empty does it take one macrotask, run it, and then loop back to check the microtasks again. That's one full turn of the loop.
So the order is almost always: synchronous code, then all promises, then timers. That's why a resolved promise always beats a zero-millisecond setTimeout.

draw.text: sync code  →  all microtasks  →  one macrotask  →  repeat
Never blocks on a slow queue — it just waits for the stack.

turns.text: Where do promises fit in?
turns.reply: Promises land in the green queue — their `.then` callbacks are microtasks, so they run before any timer.

beats.say: A promise's own executor runs synchronously, right now, on the stack. Only the .then and .catch callbacks are deferred — those become microtasks.

draw.text: executor runs sync — .then runs as a microtask

beats.say: Once the promise settles, its callback is queued here, in the microtask queue, not the orange one. Await does the same thing: everything after await is a microtask.
So they beat timers. Promise callbacks and awaits drain before the loop ever picks up a setTimeout, even one with zero delay.

draw.text: microtasks always drain before the next macrotask

turns.text: Give me an example with setTimeout.
How do git branches and merging work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: A branch in Git is just a movable pointer to a commit. Here's main, sitting on a few commits.
When you branch, Git makes a second pointer at the same commit. Now you can commit on the new branch without touching main.
Meanwhile main moves on too, with its own new commit. So the two lines have diverged from a shared ancestor, C3.
Merging brings those two lines back together. Git replays one side onto the other and creates a merge commit with two parents.
If the two sides edited different lines, Git merges automatically. If they touched the same line, you get a conflict and fix it by hand.

turns.text: What's the difference with a rebase?

beats.say: Rebase instead takes your commits and replays them one by one on top of the other branch. So here, C4 and C5 get copied onto the tip of main as brand new commits.
The old C4 and C5 are thrown away and replaced. Because of that there's no merge commit at all, so the history stays one straight line instead of branching and rejoining.
Tidy log, but rewritten history. Never rebase commits other people have already pulled, or you'll hand them a mess. Rebase your own local branch, merge anything shared.

turns.text: Walk me through what happens in a REST API request from a mobile app.
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

lesson.title: REST API Request from a Mobile App

beats.say: A REST API call is really just a conversation between your phone and a server, carried over HTTPS. Here are the two parties and the path between them.

draw.text: REST API Request from a Mobile App

beats.say: It starts when the app builds an HTTP request: a method like GET or POST, a URL identifying the resource, headers for things like auth tokens, and sometimes a JSON body.
That request goes out over the network as an HTTPS call, so TLS encrypts it in transit before anything on the internet can read it.
On the server the request is routed to a handler, which checks who you are, then reads or writes the database and shapes the result into a response.
The response comes back with a status code and a JSON payload. Two hundred means success, four hundred means you did something wrong, five hundred means the server did.
Finally the app parses that JSON, updates its UI or local cache, and the user sees the result. If the request failed, the app retries or shows an error.

turns.text: Where does authentication happen?

beats.say: Auth happens on the server side, right after routing and before any database work. That's the red diamond on the board.

draw.text: Auth = server side, before data access

beats.say: The app's only job is to attach the credential, usually a bearer token in the Authorization header, like a JWT or OAuth access token. The token itself was issued much earlier, during sign-in.
If the token is missing, expired or not allowed for that resource, the server stops there and sends back four-oh-one or four-oh-three. The query never runs.
One more layer: the server also checks the token's scopes or claims, so a logged-in user can still be blocked from someone else's data. That's authorization, as opposed to plain authentication.

turns.text: Explain recursion using factorial.
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: Recursion is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that same problem. Factorial is the classic example.
Every recursion needs a base case: a smallest input it can answer directly, with no further calls. For factorial, that's n equals zero, which is just one.
Otherwise you take one step of real work, and hand the rest to a smaller call of yourself. So factorial of four becomes four times factorial of three.
Keep unwinding down like that until you hit the base case, and then you climb back up multiplying. Four times three times two times one gives twenty-four.
Then the answers come back the other way: one, then two, then six, then twenty-four. Here's the whole thing in code.

turns.text: What's a stack overflow then?
turns.reply: It's what happens when the recursion never hits the base case — each call piles another frame onto the stack, and the stack runs out of room. Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Remember, each pending call waits on the stack for its answer. Unwinding from four down to the base case means five frames are sitting there at once.
Now imagine the base case is missing or never matches. Nothing ever stops the descent, so frames keep stacking with no answer coming back.
Eventually the stack hits its limit and the program crashes. In Python that's a RecursionError; in Java or C it's a stack overflow.
So the fix is always the same: make sure there's a reachable base case, and ideally that each call shrinks the input toward it.

turns.text: How does a compiler turn code into a program?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out — a quick flight through the pipeline.

lesson.title: How a Compiler Turns Code into a Program

beats.say: It's a pipeline: your source text goes in one end and machine code comes out the other, with several stages in between.
First the lexer chops the raw characters into tokens — names, numbers, operators. Then the parser groups those tokens into a tree that captures the grammar.
Next comes semantic analysis: the compiler checks meaning. Are the types compatible, are variables declared before use, does this function call make sense?
The middle end then builds an intermediate representation — a simple, machine-independent form — and optimizes it. Dead code gets cut, loops get tightened, so the final program is faster and smaller.
Finally the back end maps that IR onto the target CPU: it picks instructions, then allocates registers so values live in the fastest spots available.

The linker then glues your object code together with libraries and startup code, producing one executable file. Run it, and the CPU — or a virtual machine, for bytecode languages — executes those instructions at last.

turns.text: More detail on parsing.

beats.say: Parsing just here: the token stream has to be matched against the language's grammar rules, the way you'd diagram a sentence in English.
The grammar says one construct — an if statement — is a condition plus a then-branch. Parsing is the act of fitting the flat tokens into that nested shape.
Under it sit a condition node holding x greater than zero, and a body node holding the assignment. Each child is itself a small tree of operators and operands.

Two classic styles get you there: top-down recursive descent, where each grammar rule becomes a function that calls the rules below it, and bottom-up shift-reduce parsers that pile tokens on a stack until a rule fits. Recursive descent is what most hand-written compilers use.
Errors are handled right here too. A good parser reports the offending token and its line, then recovers by skipping to the next safe point so it can find more than just the first mistake.
And that tree is the handoff: the semantic checker walks it the same way the parser built it, which is why parsing is the stage everything after quietly depends on.

turns.text: How does garbage collection work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Garbage collection is how a language reclaims memory you're no longer using, so you don't have to free it by hand.
Everything starts as reachable: the program holds references to objects, and those objects point to others, forming a graph.
When you drop a reference, the object can become unreachable. Anything the roots can't reach is, by definition, garbage.
The collector walks from the roots, marks everything it can reach, then sweeps away whatever stayed unmarked and returns that memory to the free pool.

Real runtimes add tricks: reference counting frees at zero instantly but leaks cycles, while generational collectors focus on young objects since most die quickly, and compaction moves survivors together to fight fragmentation.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Let me simplify it.

beats.say: One idea, in three pictures. First: your program holds some objects by a chain from the roots.
Second: some objects nothing points to anymore. Those are garbage.
Third: the collector finds them and hands the memory back. That's the whole trick.

turns.text: Explain the MVC pattern.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: MVC splits an app into three parts: the Model holds the data and rules, the View shows it on screen, and the Controller handles the user's input.
Say you click a button. The Controller catches that input and decides what should happen next, rather than the View or the Model reacting on its own.
The Controller then talks to the Model, asking it to read or change data, and the Model enforces the rules before anything is allowed to change.
When the Model changes, it notifies the View. The View reads the fresh data and redraws itself, so what you see always matches the real state.
The win is separation: swap the View without touching the logic, test the Model alone, and reuse it behind a different screen entirely.

draw.text: One change, one place: UI, logic and input stay independent.

turns.text: Give me an example with a to-do app.
turns.reply: I'll add that to the board.

beats.say: Same three boxes, now filled in with a real to-do app, reading each one in order.
The Model is just the list of tasks, whether each one is done, and the code that saves the list. No screen and no buttons here.

draw.text: Model: list of tasks, each with text + done flag, saved to disk

beats.say: The View draws that list: a row per task, a checkbox, and a strikethrough when something is done. It never changes the data itself.

draw.text: View: the list on screen, checkboxes, strikethrough for done

beats.say: The Controller is the middleman: you type a task and hit Add, it tells the Model to add it, and the View refreshes once the Model has changed.

draw.text: Controller: handles “Add”, ticks a checkbox, deletes a task

turns.text: Show me how binary search works.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out.

beats.say: Binary search is for a sorted list. Imagine we're hunting for the number 23 in this sorted array of values.

draw.text: Binary Search: find 23 in a sorted list

beats.say: We keep two boundaries: low and high. The trick is we never look at every element, we just jump to the middle.
Look at the middle element, 23. Compare it with our target. If the middle equals the target, we're done.
Now say the target were smaller, like 9. The middle is too big, so the target must be on the left. We throw away the entire right half in one step.
We move the high marker just below the middle and repeat. Each round halves the search space, so for a million items it's about twenty comparisons, not a million.
Two things to remember. The list must be sorted, and the search space shrinks by half each time, which is why the cost is logarithmic.

turns.text: Why is it log n?

beats.say: Why log n? Because each comparison doesn't shrink the list by one item, it throws away half of what's left.
Start with n items, look at the middle. One step leaves n over 2. Two steps leave n over 4. Three steps leave n over 8.
We stop when only one item is left, that is when n over 2 to the k equals 1. Solving that gives k equals log base 2 of n. So the number of steps is the logarithm.
Concretely, doubling the data adds only one comparison. Eight items need three steps, sixteen need four, a million needs about twenty.

turns.text: What if the list isn't sorted?
turns.reply:
Short answer: binary search just gives wrong answers — you can silently skip the element you're looking for.

To fix it, sort first (O(n log n)), then search (O(log n)); or if you need speed on unsorted data, use a hash set for O(1) lookups.

turns.text: Explain quicksort.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out.

beats.say: Quicksort sorts a list by picking one item as a pivot, then splitting everything else around it. Let's use this row of numbers.
Now we choose one value as the pivot — say the last one, 2. The pivot is what everything else gets compared against.
Next comes the partition: every value smaller than the pivot goes to the left, every value bigger goes to the right. Here 1 goes left, and 3, 5, 8, 7, 4 wait on the right.
Once partitioned, the pivot is in its final place — it never moves again. Then we just repeat the same trick on the left pile and the right pile, independently.

draw.text: sort each side the same way

beats.say: That repeat-and-conquer is why it's fast: each level does about n comparisons, and a good pivot roughly halves the list, so you get about n log n work overall.

draw.text: log n levels × n work = n log n

beats.say: And that's the whole idea: pick a pivot, split smaller from bigger, park the pivot, then sort the two sides the same way. In practice it's the go-to sort for big in-memory lists.

turns.text: Show me the partition step on an example.

beats.say: Let's walk through the partition on the right pile — 3, 5, 8, 7, 4 — with 4 as the pivot this time.
We keep a boundary pointer, starting before the first element. Scanning left to right, 3 is smaller than 4, so we swap it into the boundary and move the boundary right one step.
5 is bigger than the pivot, so we leave it where it is. Nothing to do.
8 and 7 are also bigger, so they stay put too, and the boundary never moves.
Now we reach the pivot itself. We swap it with whatever sits at the boundary — here 5. So 4 lands between 3 and the big ones, and 5 jumps to the end.
Final split: 3 on the left of the pivot, 5, 8, 7 on the right, and 4 is now in its final sorted position. That's one partition done in a single pass.

turns.text: How does breadth-first search work on a graph?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Breadth-first search explores a graph in layers, closest nodes first. Here's a small graph: node A connects to B and C, B connects to D, and C connects to E.
It uses a queue, first in first out, and a visited set so no node is queued twice. We start by marking the source A visited and putting it in the queue.
We take A out of the queue and add its unvisited neighbours B and C. They go to the back of the queue, and both are marked visited.
Next we dequeue B and add its only new neighbour, D. Notice C comes out after B — that's the layer order.
Then we dequeue C and add E, and finally D and E have no new neighbours, so the queue empties. The visit order is A, B, C, D, E.

draw.text: Visit order: A -> B -> C -> D -> E

beats.say: The key property: BFS reaches every node by the shortest number of edges first. That's why it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, at the cost of memory for the queue and visited set.

turns.text: How is depth-first search different?
turns.reply: Let me add a DFS comparison to the board.

beats.say: Depth-first search keeps the same graph, but swaps the queue for a stack, last in first out, or equivalently uses recursion. So instead of finishing a whole layer, it dives down one branch as far as it can go.
Starting from A, DFS pushes B and C, then pops the most recent one. If it pops B first, it goes A to B to D, all the way down, before ever touching C or E.
So BFS uses a queue and explores level by level, while DFS uses a stack and explores branch by branch. Both mark nodes visited so nothing repeats.

The big difference in use: BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs, DFS just gives an order. DFS is lighter on memory and is the one you want for detecting cycles, topological sorting, and connectivity.

turns.text: How does a hash table handle collisions?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: A hash table turns a key into an array index with a hash function, so lookups are roughly instant. But two different keys can land on the same index — that's a collision.
Chaining is the classic fix. Each bucket holds a small list, and colliding entries just get appended to the same list.
Lookup means hashing the key, jumping to its bucket, then walking that short chain to find the match.

draw.text: lookup: index, then scan the chain

beats.say: Open addressing takes another route. There are no lists — on a collision you probe forward for the next free slot, either one step at a time or by jumping in a pattern.
The catch is load factor — how full the table is. As it fills up, chains grow long and probing takes more steps, so the table resizes and rehashes to keep things fast.

draw.text: grow when load factor gets high, then rehash

turns.text: More detail on open addressing.

beats.say: Open addressing keeps every entry in the array itself, so there are no lists at all. A collision just means the slot you wanted is taken, and you probe for the next one.
Linear probing steps one slot at a time, index plus one, plus two, and so on. It's cache friendly, but deletions are tricky and it suffers from clustering — runs of full slots get long.

To spread things out, you can probe by a quadratic step, index plus one squared, two squared, and so on, or use double hashing — a second hash function decides the step size so different keys take different paths.
Lookup works the same way: probe along the same sequence and stop when you find the key, or when you hit an empty slot — that empty slot proves the key isn't there.

draw.text: stop at the key, or at an empty slot

beats.say: Deleting is the subtle part. You can't just blank a slot, or you'd break the probe chain for keys that probed past it. Instead you leave a tombstone marker, which lookup walks over and insert can reclaim.

draw.text: delete: leave a tombstone, not an empty slot

beats.say: And because every entry lives in the array, the table has to stay sparse. Load factor is usually capped around a half to two thirds — past that, probes explode, so the table grows and rehashes.

turns.text: Explain Big O notation with examples.
turns.reply: Big O is a way of describing how an algorithm's work grows as the input gets bigger — I'll sketch it out.

beats.say: Big O notation describes how the running time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size n grows. We ignore constants and small details, and keep only the fastest-growing term — that's the growth rate that dominates for large inputs.

Here's the ladder of common complexities, from fastest-growing-work to slowest, that is, from worst to best. At the top O of n squared doubles work when you double n squared. Below it O of n log n, then linear O of n, and at the bottom the nearly flat O of log n and constant O of one.

draw.text: slower work per step ↑ / ↑ faster as n grows

beats.say: A quick concrete example for each. Getting the first item of a list is constant. Binary search on a sorted list halves the problem each time, so it's log n. Scanning one list once is linear.

draw.text: O(n): one for-loop over n items
O(n log n): merge sort, heap sort

beats.say: Take a nested loop: an outer loop over n and an inner loop over n means n times n, which is O of n squared. Bubble sort and naive duplicate-finding look like this. In code it's the two nested loops that give it away.

draw.text: for i in range(n):\n  for j in range(n):\n    ...   →  n² steps

beats.say: The key idea to remember: Big O gives an upper bound on growth, not exact seconds. So when n gets large, the algorithm's class matters far more than your machine's speed — a linear algorithm will always beat a quadratic one for big enough n.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Sure — think of Big O as "how much slower does this get as the list grows?" Doubling the list and the work stays the same is O(1), doubles is O(n), quadruples is O(n²). That's the whole idea.

turns.text: How does inserting into a linked list work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: A linked list is just nodes, and each node holds a value plus a pointer to the next node. The last node points to nothing.
Say we want to insert a new node with value X between A and B. First we walk from the head until we reach A, the node we want to insert after.

draw.text: 1. Walk from head to find node A

beats.say: Now the new node X goes in, but X's next pointer still points to nothing. If we linked A to X right now, we would lose the rest of the list.
So the order matters. Point X at B first. That keeps the tail of the list reachable.
Then point A at X. Now the chain runs A to X to B to C, and nothing was lost. That is the whole trick: new node first, then the predecessor.
The cost is just the walk. Inserting at the front is O of 1, while inserting in the middle or at the end is O of n because you must find the spot first.

draw.text: Rule: link the new node before you rewire the old one.

turns.text: How is that different from an array?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Main difference is memory layout. A linked list scatters nodes anywhere and stitches them with pointers, while an array stores its items back to back in one solid block.
To insert in the middle of an array you must shove every later element one slot right to make room, which is O of n every time. A linked list just re-points two arrows, and no data moves.

draw.text: insert: shift B, C, D right — O(n)
linked list: just re-point — no shifting

beats.say: The trade-off runs both ways. Arrays win on random access and cache locality, and you get any element by index in constant time. Linked lists win on cheap insert and delete, but you pay for it by walking from the head every time.

draw.text: array: fixed size, growing means copying
list: no O(1) index — walk to position

turns.text: How does Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm work?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out.

beats.say: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest route from one starting node to every other node in a weighted graph, where each edge has a non-negative cost.
It keeps a best-known distance for each node. The start gets zero, and everything else starts at infinity, since we haven't found a way to reach them yet.
Each round it picks the unvisited node with the smallest known distance and calls that node settled. From A, the nearest is C with cost one, so C is locked in.

Then it relaxes C's neighbours: for each one, it checks whether going through C gives a shorter path than what's already recorded, and if so, it updates that distance. Here C offers B a cost of three, but A already reaches B directly for four, so B improves to three, while D through C costs nine and stays as is.
It repeats: pick the smallest unsettled distance, settle it, relax its neighbours. B at three, then D at eight, then E at eleven, and each settled node's distance is final.

Because every edge cost is non-negative, once a node is settled no later detour can beat it, so that greedy choice is always safe. The catch is the cost must never be negative, or the guarantee breaks.

turns.text: Give me an example on a small graph.

beats.say: Let's trace a tiny five-node graph, hand-run, step by step. The graph is A, B, C, D, E, with A as the start.
Start state: A is zero, all others infinity. Every round we take the smallest unsettled value and finalize it.

draw.text: Start:   A=0, B=∞, C=∞, D=∞, E=∞   settled: {}

beats.say: Round one: C is nearest at distance one, so C is settled. Relaxing its only outgoing edge, C to D at cost eight, gives D a candidate of nine.
Round two: B at three is next. Settle B, then relax: B to C is two but C is already done at one, and B to D at five gives D a better value, three plus five equals eight.
Round three: D at eight. Settle it, then relax D to E, so E becomes eight plus three, eleven.
Round four: settle E at eleven. Done. Distances: A zero, C one, B three, D eight, E eleven. The shortest path to E is A to C to B to D to E.

draw.text: Round 4: settle E (11).  A=0  C=1  B=3  D=8  E=11

turns.text: Explain the CAP theorem.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it on the whiteboard for you.

beats.say: CAP theorem is about distributed databases. Three letters: Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance. The catch is you can only guarantee two of them at once.
Consistency means every node sees the same, latest data. A read always returns the most recent write, no matter which node answers.

draw.text: Every read sees the latest write

beats.say: Availability means every request gets a non-error response, quickly, from any node that is still up.

Partition tolerance means the system keeps working even when the network splits and nodes can't talk to each other. In the real world, networks drop messages, so partitions happen whether you like it or not.

Here is the key. A partition happens, so you must tolerate it. Now choose: answer with possibly stale data, which is Availability, or refuse and stay correct, which is Consistency. You can't have both.

draw.text: Partition: A and B can't talk

beats.say: So in practice, systems are labelled CP or AP. CP databases like HBase favour consistency and let some requests fail. AP databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB favour availability and accept eventual consistency.

draw.label: AP: always answers, may be stale

turns.text: Give me an example of a CP and an AP database.
turns.reply: Let me add those to the board.

beats.say: On the CP side, think HBase, MongoDB in its default settings, or Google Spanner. When a partition hits, they'd rather return an error or make you wait than hand you stale data.
On the AP side, Cassandra, DynamoDB, and Riak are the classics. They keep answering during a split and reconcile later, so you might read an old value for a little while.

turns.text: Microservices versus a monolith: what's the difference?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Both are ways of arranging the same app. A monolith is one deployable unit; microservices split it into many small ones that talk over the network.
Inside the monolith, all the features share one process and one database.
In microservices each capability becomes its own small service with its own database, deployed and scaled on its own.
The trade-off: microservices buy independent scaling and teams, but you pay in network calls, latency, and much harder debugging.
Rule of thumb: start as a monolith, and split out a service only when a real pain point forces it.

draw.text: Start monolith, split only when it hurts

turns.text: How do the services talk to each other?
turns.reply: I'll add that to the board.

beats.say: Two common styles: synchronous calls and asynchronous events. Let me show both beside the services.
In a synchronous call, one service asks another and waits for the answer, usually over HTTP or gRPC. Fast and simple, but if the other service is slow or down, you feel it right away.
In the asynchronous style, a service publishes an event to a message broker and moves on. Other services subscribe and react whenever they can, so nothing waits.
Either way you need retries, timeouts, and idempotency, because network calls fail and events can arrive twice.

turns.text: How does a message queue like Kafka work?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Kafka is a log, not a traditional queue. Producers append messages to the end of an ordered, append-only log, and each message gets a sequential offset number.
A topic is split into partitions so it can scale. Each partition is independent and ordered, and messages are spread across them by a key, so the same key always lands in the same partition.
Consumers read by pulling, and they track their own position with an offset. Unlike a queue, reading does not delete the message — it stays in the log for a retention period.
Consumers in a group split the partitions among themselves, so each partition is handled by exactly one consumer in that group — that is how Kafka scales out horizontally.
Under the hood, brokers form a cluster and each partition has one leader and followers that replicate it. If a broker dies, a follower takes over as leader, which is where the durability comes from.

turns.text: What's a consumer group?
turns.reply: Let me zoom in on that part of the board.

beats.say: A consumer group is just a team of consumers that share the work of one topic. Every partition is assigned to exactly one member of the group, so the group reads a partition once, in order.

draw.text: One partition → one consumer per group

beats.say: With three partitions you can have up to three useful consumers. Add a fourth and it just sits idle, because there is no partition left to hand out.

draw.text: One partition → one consumer per group

beats.say: What makes it powerful is that groups are independent. A payments group and an analytics group can each read the same topic from start to finish, without stealing anything from each other.

draw.text: reads the same log, own offsets

beats.say: If one consumer crashes, Kafka rebalances and hands its partitions to the survivors. If you want pause, continue, replay, or next, just say so.

turns.text: How does a database index make queries faster?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out — a quick drawing beats a paragraph here.

lesson.title: How a database index speeds up queries

beats.say: Start with a table of rows sitting on disk, and a query asking for one specific value.

draw.text: Indexes: fewer rows to look at

beats.say: Without an index the engine scans every row, top to bottom, until it stumbles on a match.
An index is a sorted side structure, usually a B-tree, keyed on the column you search by.
The search compares against the sorted keys and walks down a handful of levels, discarding half the remaining rows at each step.
The leaf holds the pointer straight to the row, so the query jumps there instead of reading the table at all.

turns.text: More detail on the B-tree.
turns.reply: I'll add a zoomed-in look at the B-tree on the free space to the right.

beats.say: Zoom in: each B-tree node is a small block holding a sorted list of keys — say up to a few hundred of them.

draw.text: one node = up to N sorted keys

beats.say: Between the keys sit child pointers: everything below a pointer falls in that key range. Forty-three lands in the middle range, so we follow just that one child.

draw.text: one node = up to N sorted keys

beats.say: The lowest level holds the leaves, with the actual row pointers, and neighbouring leaves are linked — that's why range queries and sorting stay cheap too.

draw.text: leaves linked: range scans walk in order

beats.say: Because each node fans out into hundreds of children, the tree stays only three or four levels deep for millions of rows, and writes rebalance it so it never degenerates.

draw.text: high fan-out -> shallow tree: 3-4 levels for millions of rows
each level = 1 page read, usually cached in RAM
kept balanced on insert/delete, so depth never grows into a line

turns.text: How does caching with Redis in front of a database work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch this out for you.

lesson.title: Redis Cache in Front of a Database

beats.say: Here's the basic setup: your app talks to Redis first, and only falls back to the database when Redis doesn't have the answer.

draw.text: Redis Cache in Front of a DB

beats.say: A read hits Redis first. On a cache hit, Redis returns the value in microseconds and the database is never touched — that's the whole point.

draw.text: HIT: return value fast, DB untouched

beats.say: On a miss, the app queries the database, gets the row, and writes it back into Redis with a time-to-live so stale data expires on its own. The very next request is a hit.

draw.text: MISS: query DB → store in Redis with a TTL
TTL = safety net against stale data

beats.say: Writes are the tricky part. You can write to the database and then delete the cache key so the next read repopulates it, or write to both — but you have to pick a strategy and be consistent.
A few things bite people in practice: the first burst after a restart stampedes the database, hot keys can overload one Redis node, and data can go stale between a write and the invalidation.

draw.text: Watch out: cache stampede, hot keys, staleness windows

beats.say: And the payoff: Redis absorbs the vast majority of reads in memory, so your database only sees misses and writes, which is what lets it scale.

draw.text: Result: DB load drops to misses + writes

turns.text: What's cache invalidation?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out.

beats.say: Cache invalidation is just deciding when a cached copy stops being trusted. There are only two real mechanisms: time and events.

draw.text: Cache invalidation = when to stop trusting the copy

beats.say: Time-based is the TTL you already have. You don't decide anything per write — the key simply expires, and the worst case is data that's stale for at most the TTL.

draw.text: TIME-BASED: key expires after TTL · simple, bounded staleness

beats.say: Event-based invalidation deletes or updates the key the moment the data changes. That's the write path on the right — fresher data, but every writer has to remember to do it.

draw.text: EVENT-BASED: delete/update key on write · fresher, more moving parts

beats.say: The usual failure is a window: you write to the database, and before the cache key is deleted, a read sneaks in and re-caches the old value. Now the stale entry sits there until the TTL saves you.

draw.text: The bad window: read re-caches old value before invalidation

beats.say: So in practice you use both: invalidate on write for freshness, and keep a TTL as the backstop for anything you missed. Most people call the combination delete-on-write plus TTL.

draw.text: Practical answer: delete on write + TTL as the backstop

turns.text: How are Docker containers different from virtual machines?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Both run your app in an isolated box. The difference is how much they carry, so let's start from the hardware at the bottom and build up two stacks side by side.
A virtual machine has its own full guest operating system, complete with its own kernel. Above that sits a hypervisor, which carves the physical machine into separate virtual computers.
A container skips the guest operating system entirely. All containers share the host's single kernel, so all you ship is your app plus its libraries.
That missing layer explains the speed. A container starts in milliseconds and weighs megabytes, while a VM boots in tens of seconds and carries gigabytes of operating system.
Isolation runs the other way: a VM is a hard wall because the guest kernel sits between your code and the host, while containers share that kernel, so a kernel bug can leak across them.
So in practice: use containers for your services and fast deployments, and virtual machines when you need a different operating system or a much harder boundary between tenants.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: I'll simplify it to the one core idea.

beats.say: One line: a virtual machine is a whole computer, and a container is just your app in a box. That's the whole difference.
A VM brings its own operating system, so it's big and slow to start. A container borrows the one you already have, so it's small and fast.
Rule of thumb: need a different operating system or really strong walls, use a VM. Otherwise a container is almost always fine.

turns.text: How would you design a URL shortener?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out.

beats.say: At its core a URL shortener is just a lookup service: a short code maps to a long URL. The two main flows are creating a short link, and resolving one when someone clicks it.

The database is the heart of it: short_code as the primary key, the long URL as the value, plus a bit of metadata like creation time and expiry. It's a read-heavy workload, so you cache hot codes in memory.

For generating codes, the usual trick is a counter encoded in base 62 — digits, upper and lowercase — which gives you 62 to the 7th, roughly three and a half trillion codes in seven characters. A hash like MD5 truncated to seven chars also works, but you risk collisions.

A distributed counter needs ranges handed out to each node so they don't collide. For reads, you want a redirect at the edge — a cache or CDN holds popular codes so most clicks never touch the database.
Resolving should return a 301 redirect, which browsers cache, or 302 if you want accurate click analytics. Beyond that you'd add rate limiting, custom aliases, and analytics on click counts.

turns.text: How do you handle lots of traffic?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Resolution traffic is almost all reads, so the first move is to keep clicks far away from the database. The CDN and cache absorb the vast majority of them, and only misses fall through to the store.

Behind the API you put a load balancer and run many stateless API instances. Because they hold no state, you just add more when traffic grows — and the long URLs are also immutable, so any replica can serve any read.

The key-value store scales by sharding, for example on the first characters of the short code. That spreads writes and keeps lookups a single hop. Replication adds read capacity and keeps you serving if a node dies.

The counter is the one piece that's hard to distribute, so keep it out of the hot path: allocate ranges up front and hand them to nodes, and a web-tier cache means one hit warms thousands of requests. Analytics should be fire-and-forget into a queue rather than written synchronously on every click.

turns.text: What does ACID mean for database transactions?
turns.reply: I'll sketch this one out for you.

beats.say: ACID is four guarantees a database makes about a transaction, usually a group of statements treated as one unit.
A is atomicity: the transaction happens completely or not at all. If it fails halfway, every change is rolled back.
C is consistency: the data moves from one valid state to another, with all rules and constraints still satisfied.
I is isolation: concurrent transactions don't step on each other. It looks like they ran one after another.
D is durability: once committed, the change survives a crash or power loss, because it's written to disk.
So together: one unit, valid rules, no interference, and permanent once committed — that's what ACID promises.

draw.text: One unit · valid state · no interference · permanent

turns.text: Give me a bank transfer example.
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Take a transfer of a hundred dollars from Alice to Bob. Two statements: debit Alice, credit Bob — and both must be Atomic.
Atomicity: if the credit fails after the debit, the whole thing rolls back — Alice keeps her hundred. No money vanishes.
Consistency: a constraint says balances can't go negative. If Alice only has fifty, the transfer is rejected and the totals still add up.
Isolation: while this runs, another transfer on the same accounts waits or sees the old values — never a half-done state.
Durability: once it commits, the new balances survive a crash, so the bank statement stays correct.

turns.text: Explain process states in an operating system.
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out.

beats.say: A process is just a running program, and the OS tracks it through a handful of states. Let's start with the two you can't avoid: New, when the process is being created, and Ready, when it's loaded and waiting for CPU time.

draw.text: Process States in an Operating System

beats.say: From Ready, the scheduler picks it and it becomes Running — now it actually owns the CPU and its instructions execute. From Running it can go back to Ready if its time slice runs out.
Often the process can't continue — it asks for a file, or waits on input. Then it moves to Waiting or Blocked, off the CPU entirely until the event it wanted happens.
Finally, when the process finishes or is killed, it goes to Terminated and the OS reclaims its memory and resources.

The key insight is that only one process per core is ever Running, while many can sit in Ready or Waiting at once. The OS keeps a queue for each state and moves processes between them — that dance is what we call scheduling.

draw.text: One Running per core; many Ready and Waiting. The OS moves processes between state queues.

turns.text: What makes a process go to waiting?

lesson.title: What Sends a Process to Waiting

beats.say: A process goes to Waiting whenever it can't proceed on its own — it's blocked on something outside the CPU. Let's list the usual culprits next to the Running state.

draw.text: • I/O request: reading a file, a network packet, a keypress
• Waiting on a lock, mutex or semaphore held by another process
• Waiting for another process to finish, or for a timer / sleep to expire

beats.say: The pattern is the same in every case: a system call or event the process can't control. Two important details — the process does not choose to wait, the OS blocks it; and a page fault usually does not send it here, the OS just fetches the page and resumes it.

draw.text: Not chosen by the process — the OS blocks it. Page faults usually resume silently.

turns.text: Explain photosynthesis.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it on the whiteboard for you.

beats.say: Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food, turning light into sugar. Let's start with the two ingredients they take in.
Carbon dioxide comes in from the air through tiny leaf pores, and water is pulled up from the roots.
Inside the leaf sits chlorophyll, the green pigment that captures sunlight — the third ingredient.
Light energy from the sun drives the reaction that joins the carbon dioxide and water together.
The plant ends up with glucose — its food and building material — and releases oxygen as a bonus.
In short: carbon dioxide plus water plus light gives glucose plus oxygen. That's the whole trick, and it feeds nearly every food chain on Earth.

turns.text: Simpler, please.

beats.say: Okay, simpler. Two things go in: air and water.
And the sun gives the plant energy to do it.
That's it: air, water and sun become food, and the plant breathes out oxygen. Simple as that.

turns.text: What happens in the dark reactions?

beats.say: The dark reactions, or Calvin cycle, are the second half of the job. They don't need light themselves, but they do need the energy the light reactions captured.

draw.label: uses CO2 + the energy from the light step

beats.say: They grab carbon dioxide from the air and use that stored energy to build it into glucose, the plant's food.

turns.text: Explain the water cycle.
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: The water cycle is Earth's way of recycling water — the same water moves between the ocean, the sky and the land, over and over.
Heat from the sun makes water evaporate from the ocean and lakes, rising as invisible vapour. Plants add more through transpiration.
High up, the air is cold, so the vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds.
When the droplets get heavy enough, they fall as precipitation — rain, snow, sleet or hail.
On land the water soaks into the soil as infiltration, or runs downhill as runoff, back toward the ocean and lakes.
And that water eventually evaporates again — so the cycle never stops, and it's the same water going round and round.

turns.text: Where do clouds come from exactly?
turns.reply: Good question — that's the condensation step, so let me zoom in on the cloud and show that bit on the board.

beats.say: Warm air near the surface is full of invisible water vapour. As it rises, it expands and cools — and cool air can't hold as much vapour as warm air.

draw.text: Rising air cools as it expands

beats.say: Once it cools to the dew point, the vapour condenses onto tiny particles called condensation nuclei — specks of dust, sea salt and smoke floating in the air.

draw.text: Condensation nuclei: dust, sea salt, smoke

beats.say: Those droplets are around a hundredth of a millimetre across, and each one is far tinier than a raindrop. Billions of them together are what you see as a cloud.
Inside the cloud, droplets collide and grow. Once they're heavy enough that rising air can't hold them up, they fall as rain or snow — the precipitation step we drew before.

turns.text: How does mitosis work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Mitosis is how one cell divides into two identical cells. It's the process behind growth and healing, and it happens in four main stages.
First the cell copies its DNA, so it has two identical sets of chromosomes. Then those copies get pulled to opposite ends of the cell.

draw.text: DNA is copied, then pulled apart

beats.say: Next, the cell pinches in the middle and splits into two. Each new cell ends up with one full set of chromosomes.
So the end result is two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the original. That's what lets you heal a cut or grow from one cell into a whole body.

turns.text: How is meiosis different?
turns.reply: I'll add meiosis alongside it.

beats.say: Meiosis starts the same way, with one cell copying its DNA, but it divides twice instead of once. So you end up with four cells instead of two.

draw.text: each cell gets half the DNA

beats.say: The big difference is what those four cells are. During meiosis the chromosomes get shuffled, so each one is genetically unique rather than a copy, and the halves meet up again as an egg and a sperm.

draw.text: chromosomes are shuffled, so every cell is unique

beats.say: So put simply: mitosis makes two identical cells for growth and repair, while meiosis makes four different cells with half the DNA, for reproduction.

draw.text: Mitosis: for growth and repair. Meiosis: for making eggs and sperm.

turns.text: How does blood flow through the heart?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: The heart is really two pumps side by side: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side sends it to the body. Each pump has an upper collecting chamber, an atrium, and a lower pumping chamber, a ventricle.
Deoxygenated blood returns from the body into the right atrium, then drops down through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and turns bright red.
Fresh oxygenated blood comes back into the left atrium, and passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, the strongest chamber.
Finally the left ventricle blasts that blood out through the aortic valve into the aorta, which carries it to every part of the body. Then the loop starts again.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Let me boil it down on the board.

beats.say: Simple version. One loop, six stops. First half: blood from the body goes to the right atrium, then the right ventricle, then the lungs to pick up oxygen.
Second half: from the lungs it goes to the left atrium, then the left ventricle, then out to the body. And then it all loops back to the start.

turns.text: What's the structure of an atom?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: An atom is the basic unit of matter, and it has just two main regions: a tiny dense core, and a big fuzzy cloud around it.
Inside the nucleus sit protons, which are positive, and neutrons, which are neutral. Together they make up almost all the atom's mass.
Around the nucleus, electrons zoom around in shells, or energy levels. Each electron carries a negative charge.
Here's the key idea: the nucleus is about a hundred thousand times smaller than the whole atom, yet it holds nearly all the mass. Most of an atom is empty space.
So: protons and neutrons in the centre, electrons in shells outside, and the balance of protons to electrons decides what element it is and whether it's charged.

turns.text: What's an isotope?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: An isotope is a version of an element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
Take hydrogen. Plain hydrogen has one proton and no neutrons. Add one neutron and you get deuterium; add two and you get tritium.
Since the proton count doesn't change, it's still hydrogen, so it's still the same element. Only the mass changes.
One more thing: some isotopes are stable, and some are radioactive and slowly decay. That's what carbon-14 dating relies on.

draw.text: Some stable; some radioactive (e.g. carbon-14 dating)

turns.text: How does the greenhouse effect work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Sunlight comes in as short-wave radiation and mostly passes straight through the atmosphere.
The surface warms up and re-emits that energy as longer-wave infrared, heading back out toward space.
Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb much of that infrared instead of letting it escape.
They then re-radiate it in all directions, and the portion sent back down adds extra heat to the surface.
That trapping of outgoing heat is the greenhouse effect; a natural amount keeps Earth about 33 degrees warmer than it would otherwise be.

draw.text: Natural effect: ~+33 C. Extra gases = extra warming.

turns.text: More detail on which gases matter.
turns.reply: I'll add the main gases and their contributions.

beats.say: The big one by sheer amount is water vapour, which alone accounts for roughly half to two-thirds of the natural warming.
Then carbon dioxide, which matters less per molecule but is what we add most of by burning fossil fuels, so it drives most of the human-made warming.
Per molecule, methane traps far more heat than CO2, and fluorinated gases more still, though there is very little of them.

draw.text: Potency per molecule: CO2 < methane < N2O < fluorinated

beats.say: It is really about balance: more of these gases means more infrared re-radiated back, and the surface keeps warming.

draw.text: More gases = more heat trapped = more warming.

turns.text: How do vaccines train the immune system?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

lesson.title: How Vaccines Train the Immune System

beats.say: A vaccine is basically a training manual for your immune system. It shows your body a harmless preview of a germ, so the real thing never catches you off guard.

draw.text: How vaccines train the immune system
Weak, dead or just a protein piece

beats.say: The key ingredient is the antigen, a distinctive marker on the germ's surface. Your immune cells read that marker and recognise it as foreign.

draw.text: Shows the marker to other immune cells

beats.say: Then the alarm goes out. Helper T cells coordinate the response, and B cells that match the antigen start producing antibodies that lock onto it.
This is where the training really pays off. Some cells become memory B and T cells that stay behind for years, remembering that exact marker.
Months later, if the real germ shows up, those memory cells respond within days instead of weeks. Antibodies swarm fast and clear the infection before you feel much of anything.

turns.text: Why do some need boosters?
turns.reply: I'll add that to the board.

beats.say: Two things fade over time: antibody levels in your blood, and the number of memory cells. Nothing is wrong — the training just gets a little quiet.

draw.text: Weak, dead or just a protein piece
Antibodies and memory cells slowly decline

beats.say: A booster dose re-exposes you to the same antigen. The second time around the response is faster and much bigger — that's why the graph jumps higher.

Some vaccines also need several primary doses to build a strong enough first response, like tetanus or HPV. Others are needed because the virus mutates quickly, so the target marker changes — that's the flu and COVID situation.

turns.text: What's the difference between series and parallel circuits?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: Let's compare the two basic ways to wire components together, starting with a series circuit.
In a series circuit everything sits on one loop, so the same current flows through each component in turn.
Now a parallel circuit. Components branch across the same two points, so each gets its own path.
Here the voltage across each branch is the same, but the current splits between the branches.
The practical difference: in series one failure breaks the whole loop, while in parallel the other branches keep working. That's why old fairy lights went dark and homes are wired in parallel.

turns.text: Which one do houses use?
turns.reply: Houses are wired in parallel, so each light and outlet gets the full mains voltage and keeps working when one fails.

beats.say: This is the parallel side, and it's the one your house uses.
Every branch sees the same voltage, so a lamp, a fridge and a phone charger all get the full supply regardless of what else is on.

draw.text: Whole house: parallel branches off one supply

beats.say: Switching something on just adds another path, and it doesn't change the others, which is why the kitchen light doesn't flicker when the kettle boils.

turns.text: Explain a food chain and energy transfer.
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: A food chain is just a line of who eats whom, and energy travels along it in one direction.
Plants are the producers: they capture sunlight and store it as food. Everything else in the chain depends on that.
Each eater is a consumer, and we count them in levels, called trophic levels.

draw.text: Trophic levels: producer → primary → secondary → tertiary consumer

beats.say: Here's the key idea: only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next level. The rest is used for living or lost as heat.
So energy shrinks fast at every step — which is why food chains are short, and why there are far more plants than top predators.

turns.text: Why is only 10 percent passed on?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Good question. Most of the energy an animal eats never becomes its body — it's spent just staying alive.
Some is used in respiration for movement and keeping warm. That energy leaves as heat and is gone for good.
Only the last box, the new tissue, is what the next animal can eat. Since it's a small slice of the total, roughly a tenth carries over.
So the ten percent rule isn't a law of physics, just a rough average across many food chains.

draw.text: A rough average, not an exact law — it varies by animal

turns.text: Why do we have seasons?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Here's the Sun on the left, and Earth to its right. The key is that Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, and that tilt always points the same way in space.
In June, the northern half leans toward the Sun. Sunlight hits it more directly and days are longer, so the northern hemisphere gets summer, while the south leans away and gets winter.
Half a year later, Earth is on the other side of its orbit. The tilt hasn't changed, but now the northern half leans away from the Sun.
So the sunlight arrives at a slant and the days are short. That's winter in the north and summer in the south, since the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres.
The big myth is that seasons come from our distance to the Sun. In fact Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter. It's the tilt that does it.

draw.text: Fact: it's the 23.5° tilt, not distance. Earth is closest to the Sun in January.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Let me sketch a simpler version.

beats.say: Simply: Earth is tilted, not straight up. It's like holding a globe leaning to one side.

draw.text: Tilted, always leaning the same way

beats.say: In June the top of the globe leans toward the Sun, so the top half gets summer. In December it leans away, so the top half gets winter.

draw.text: June: top leans toward the Sun → summer up top
December: top leans away → winter up top

beats.say: Distance isn't the reason. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January, in the middle of northern winter.

turns.text: Explain supply and demand.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Supply and demand is how a market finds a price. We draw price up the side and quantity along the bottom.
Demand slopes down: when the price is low, buyers want more; when it's high, they want less.
Supply slopes up: at high prices, sellers are happy to make and sell more; at low prices, less.
Where the two lines cross is the market equilibrium. That price is where the amount buyers want exactly equals the amount sellers offer.
If the price sits above equilibrium, there's a surplus and sellers cut prices. Below it, a shortage pushes prices up. Either way, the market drifts back to the crossing point.

turns.text: What happens when demand goes up?

beats.say: Good question. When demand goes up, the whole demand curve shifts to the right — buyers want more at every price, not just at a low one.
At the old equilibrium price, there's now a shortage, so buyers bid against each other and the price starts climbing.
The new crossing point sits up and to the right of the old one — so a demand increase pushes both the price and the quantity higher.

turns.text: How does compound interest work?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Compound interest is interest that earns interest. You start with some money, called the principal, and each period interest is added to it.
In year one, ten percent interest adds a hundred dollars. Now the balance is eleven hundred.
Here's the key bit: in year two the interest is calculated on eleven hundred, not on your original thousand. So you earn a hundred and ten.
That extra ten dollars is interest on interest, and it snowballs. By year ten you'd have about fifteen hundred and ninety, and by year thirty more than seventeen thousand.
The shortcut formula is A equals P times one plus r over n, all raised to n times t. P is your starting amount, r the rate, n how often it compounds per year, and t the years.

draw.text: P = principal  ·  r = rate  ·  n = compounds/year  ·  t = years

beats.say: Two things matter most: time, because the curve bends upward late, and how often it compounds, since more frequent compounding means slightly faster growth.

turns.text: Give me an example with 10,000 rupees at 8 percent.

beats.say: Let's run your numbers: ten thousand rupees at eight percent a year. In year one you earn eight hundred rupees, taking you to ten thousand eight hundred.
Year two is where it bites: eight percent of ten thousand eight hundred is eight hundred and sixty-four, giving eleven thousand six hundred and sixty-four.
Give it twenty years and you'd have about forty-six thousand six hundred rupees. Notice that's roughly four point six times your money, purely from time.

And if the interest were compounded monthly instead of yearly, you'd actually end up with a little more: about forty-nine thousand two hundred and sixty-eight. More frequent compounding, slightly more money.

turns.text: What causes inflation?
turns.reply:
Inflation is basically too much money chasing too few goods — prices rise when demand outpaces what an economy can actually supply, or when the cost of producing things goes up.

Let me sketch the main causes for you.

beats.say: Inflation just means the general price level is rising, so your money buys less over time. There are a few distinct engines behind it.
First, demand-pull: when people, businesses and governments spend more than the economy can produce, buyers bid prices up.

draw.text:
Spending outruns supply,
so buyers bid prices up

beats.say: Second, cost-push: when inputs like energy, wages or shipping get more expensive, firms pass those costs on to customers.

draw.text:
Higher energy, wages
