or shipping get passed on

beats.say: Third, expectations and the money supply: if people expect rising prices they demand higher wages, and too much new money amplifies all of it.

draw.text:
Expected inflation drives
wage demands; too much
money amplifies it

beats.say: These feed back on each other, which is why central banks raise interest rates to cool spending and anchor expectations.

turns.text: How do interest rates fight it?
turns.reply: I'll add that onto the same board.

beats.say: Remember the teal box: the central bank raises its policy rate. That rate ripples out to every other loan in the economy.
First, it gets more expensive to borrow, so mortgages, car loans and business credit slow down and households save instead of spend.

draw.text:
Higher energy, wages
or shipping get passed on

beats.say: That cools demand-pull: with spending no longer outrunning supply, the bidding war for scarce goods fades.
A stronger currency and softer demand also ease imported input costs, nudging cost-push down too.
And because people see the bank acting, expected inflation falls, so wage demands moderate. That is the third engine calming.
Two cautions: the effect lags by months, and if rates go too far it tips the economy into recession. So it is a blunt, slow tool.

draw.text: Slow: lags of months. Blunt: too far = recession

turns.text: How does a UPI payment go from my phone to the shop?
turns.reply: I'll sketch the whole journey for you.

beats.say: Here's the cast: your phone with a UPI app, the NPCI switch that runs UPI, and the shop's bank. Your own bank sits on your side as the payer's bank.

draw.text: How a UPI payment reaches the shop

beats.say: You scan the shop's QR code. That code carries a VPA, something like shop@bank, which is just a nickname pointing at the shop's account. Your app builds a collect request: pay this amount to this VPA.
You approve with your UPI PIN. That PIN never leaves your phone to be checked by the shop — your app signs the request, and your bank validates the PIN and debits your account.
NPCI is the referee in the middle. It reads the VPA, finds which bank owns it, and relays the request to the shop's bank with its own settlement records.
The shop's bank credits the account, and the success message races back down the same path. The money moves instantly, but the actual bank-to-bank settlement happens later in batches.

draw.text: Real money settles later, in batches between banks

turns.text: Where is the PIN checked?
turns.reply: The PIN is verified by your own bank, never by the shop or NPCI.

lesson.title: Where the UPI PIN is checked

beats.say: When you type your UPI PIN, the app on your phone scrambles it into a cryptographic signature. The raw PIN stays inside your handset — it's never sent in readable form.

draw.text: PIN typed -> signed on the phone (PIN never uploaded raw)

beats.say: Your bank is the only party that holds your PIN reference. It decrypts the signed request and either accepts or rejects it — that check on the blue arrow is the debit step. NPCI and the shop's bank only ever see a pass-or-fail token, not your PIN.

draw.text: PIN checked HERE, at the issuer bank

beats.say: So the flow is phone, your bank, NPCI, shop's bank — and the PIN check is the first stop, keeping the secret entirely on your side of the fence.

turns.text: How does buying a share on the stock market work?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out for you.

beats.say: Say you want to buy one share of a company. You don't go to the company itself — you go to a brokerage, the app or website that acts as your middleman.

draw.text: Buying a Share: The Path of an Order

beats.say: You place an order: which share, and how many. A market order just means 'whatever the current price is' — a limit order says 'don't pay above this price'.

draw.text: Order: which share, how many, market or limit

beats.say: The broker passes that order to an exchange — a marketplace like the NYSE or Nasdaq, where buyers and sellers meet. It's basically an auction running all day.
On the exchange, your buy order gets matched against someone selling. A matching engine pairs them at a price you both accept, and that trade is now done.
Then the unglamorous part: settlement. In the US, cash and shares officially change hands one business day later, and the share is recorded in your name at your broker.

draw.text: Settlement: cash and shares swap, usually T+1 (next business day)

beats.say: So the short version: you order through a broker, the broker routes it to an exchange, the exchange matches you with a seller at an agreed price, and a day later it's officially yours — minus a small commission or fee.

draw.text: Price moves constantly — you get whatever the match happens at

turns.text: Simpler, please.

beats.say: Simplest way to think of it: you're just placing an order with an app, and the app finds someone willing to sell at a price you both accept.
That's it. The exchange is just the market where those two orders bump into each other — no haggling, the computer does it in a blink.
Money leaves your account, the share shows up in your account, usually by the next day. That's the whole thing.
One catch worth knowing: the price moves by the second, so the price you see when you tap buy might not be the exact price you get.

draw.text: Order: which share, how many, market or limit
Settlement: cash and shares swap, usually T+1 (next business day)

turns.text: Explain the Pythagorean theorem.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: The Pythagorean theorem is about right-angled triangles: triangles with one ninety-degree corner.
The two short sides that meet at the right angle are called the legs. The long side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse.
Now picture a square built on each side. Their areas are a-squared, b-squared, and c-squared.
Here's the punchline: the two smaller squares together exactly fill the big one. So a-squared plus b-squared equals c-squared.
The classic example is three, four, five. Three-squared is nine, four-squared is sixteen, and together they make twenty-five, which is five-squared.

turns.text: Show me why it's true.

beats.say: Here's the neat trick: take one big square whose side is a plus b, and put four copies of our triangle inside it.
The tilted hole left in the middle is itself a square, with side length c — that's the hypotenuse of each triangle.
Now count the same area the other way. The big square is a plus b, all squared, which is a-squared plus two a-b, plus b-squared.
The four triangles give us two a-b between them, so those terms cancel, and we're left with a-squared plus b-squared equals c-squared.
That's the whole proof — no measurement needed. It's true for every right triangle, however lopsided. Want me to try it with another number?

turns.text: Give me an example with numbers.

beats.say: The most famous one is three, four, five: nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and the square root of twenty-five is exactly five.
Any multiple of three-four-five works too, like six, eight, ten. And if you're missing the hypotenuse, you just take the square root of the sum.
Some other whole-number triples are five, twelve, thirteen and eight, fifteen, seventeen. Random sides like two, three, four don't work — the numbers have to agree.
That's the practical power of it: if the sums match, you've definitely got a right angle. That's how builders square a corner.

draw.text: So the theorem also tells you which triples are right triangles.

turns.text: What is a derivative in calculus?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out for you.

beats.say: A derivative is just a rate of change — how fast something is changing at one exact instant. Think of a car's position over time: the derivative at any moment is the speed shown on its speedometer right then.

Take two nearby points on the curve and draw a line through them. The steepness of that line — rise over run — is the average rate of change between them. Slide the two points closer together and the line pivots into the tangent line at a single point.
In the limit, as the gap shrinks to zero, that secant line becomes the tangent line touching the curve at just one point. Its slope is the derivative — the instantaneous rate of change there.
Formally, we write it as the limit of the difference quotient as h goes to zero. And there's a shortcut: the power rule says the derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus one.
So a derivative answers one question everywhere on the curve: how steeply is this changing right here? That's why it powers speed, slopes, growth rates, and optimization.

draw.text: One question: how fast is it changing right here?

turns.text: Give me the derivative of x squared step by step.
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

lesson.title: Derivative of x squared, step by step

beats.say: Let's do x squared from the limit definition, using the old board's formula. Start with f of x equals x squared, and nudge x by a small h.
Expand the square: x plus h, squared, gives x squared plus 2xh plus h squared. Subtract the original x squared and those cancel, leaving 2xh plus h squared.
Now divide by h. The h cancels and the difference quotient is just 2x plus h.

Finally let h shrink to zero: the leftover h vanishes and we're left with 2x. The slope at a point x is exactly 2x — steep and negative on the left, zero at the origin, steep and positive on the right.

turns.text: Explain Ohm's law.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out.

beats.say: Ohm's law links three things in any circuit: voltage, current and resistance. Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is what fights the flow.
The law says the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it, for a fixed resistance. So double the voltage and you double the current.
Written as an equation, voltage equals current times resistance: V equals I times R.

draw.text: I = V / R      R = V / I

beats.say: You can rearrange it two ways. To find current, divide voltage by resistance. To find resistance, divide voltage by current.
A quick example: a 12-volt supply across a 4-ohm resistor pushes 3 amps through it. That's just 12 divided by 4.

turns.text: Solve an example: 12 volts across 4 ohms.
turns.reply: That's exactly the example on the board — 12 volts across 4 ohms gives 3 amps.

beats.say: Let's run your numbers. The 12-volt source and the 4-ohm resistor are already on the board.
Start from current equals voltage divided by resistance, so 12 volts over 4 ohms.
Twelve divided by four is three, so the current is 3 amps.
Check it the other way: 3 amps times 4 ohms brings you right back to 12 volts, so the numbers agree.

turns.text: How do I solve a quadratic equation?
turns.reply: Let me sketch it out.

beats.say: A quadratic equation has the form ax squared plus bx plus c equals zero, where a isn't zero.
The formula solves every one: x equals negative b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four ac, all over two a.
The part under the root is the discriminant. If it's positive you get two answers, zero gives one, and negative gives none on the real number line.
Sometimes factoring is faster: for x² plus 5x plus 6, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5, giving x plus 2 and x plus 3.
Either way, once you have the roots, check them by putting them back into the original equation.

turns.text: Solve x squared minus 5x plus 6 equals zero.

beats.say: Here a is one, b is negative five, and c is six. So we need two numbers that multiply to six and add to negative five.
Minus two and minus three do it: they multiply to six and add to negative five.
So the factors are x minus two and x minus three, and each bracket set to zero gives the roots.
The roots are x equals two and x equals three. Checking in the formula: the discriminant is twenty-five minus twenty-four, which is one, so two real roots — confirmed.

turns.text: Explain probability with two coin flips.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Let's flip two coins and see what probability really means. It's just counting the equally likely outcomes and asking how many match what we want.
With two flips there are four possible outcomes, and every one is equally likely. We can list them all out.
Probability is just a fraction. The number of outcomes we care about, divided by the total number of outcomes — the one, two, three, four in the sample space.
Say we want exactly one head. Outcomes HT and TH match, so that's two out of four — one half, or fifty percent.
Now two heads. Only HH works, so that's one out of four — twenty five percent. And at least one head: HH, HT, TH — three out of four, or seventy five percent.

turns.text: What about three flips?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Three flips is the same idea, just bigger. Each flip doubles the outcomes, so two flips gave four, and three flips give eight.
Here are the other four. Together all eight are equally likely, so each single one has probability one eighth.
Let's ask the same question: exactly two heads. HHT, HTH and THH — that's three of the eight, or thirty seven and a half percent.
And the pattern: the counts one two three are three, three, one — that's row four of Pascal's triangle, over two to the power three.

turns.text: How do you add fractions with different denominators?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out.

beats.say: The big rule: you can only add fractions when the bottom numbers, the denominators, are the same. Here we have one half plus one third, and those bottoms don't match.
Step one is to find a common denominator, a number both 2 and 3 divide into. The smallest one is 6.
Step two, rewrite each fraction with that denominator. Half becomes three sixths, and one third becomes two sixths.
Now the bottoms match, so you just add the tops: 3 plus 2 is 5, over 6. So one half plus one third equals five sixths.

turns.text: Simpler, please.
turns.reply: Sure — let me put a simpler version up.

beats.say: Three steps. First, make the bottoms the same, here 6. Then change each fraction: a half becomes three sixths, a third becomes two sixths. Last, just add the tops, 3 plus 2 is 5, so the answer is five sixths.

turns.text: Where does pi come from?
turns.reply: Let me sketch that out.

beats.say: Pi isn't a number someone invented — it's the ratio every circle shares: the distance around a circle divided by the distance across it.

draw.text: Pi is a ratio, not an invention

beats.say: Measure any circle in the universe — a coin, a planet, a ripple in water — and C divided by d always lands on the same number, a bit over three.
That constancy is a fact of flat geometry. Curves and circles force this number to exist whether or not any human is around to notice it.
People got close estimates early: Babylonians used about 3.125, and Archimedes squeezed it between polygons inscribed in and around a circle to pin it near 3.14.
Later, with calculus and infinite series, we could compute pi to any precision — but that's just more digits of a number that was already there.

turns.text: How do I use it for the area of a circle?

lesson.title: Pi and the area of a circle

beats.say: Same circle, same pi — the relationship that gave us the circumference also gives us the area, just with the radius instead.
Here's why the radius and the square show up. Cut the circle into thin wedges, like slicing a pizza into many skinny pieces.
Now alternate the wedges point-up, point-down. The more slices, the more the shape becomes a rectangle — its height is r, the radius.

draw.text: width = half the circumference = pi r

beats.say: The rectangle's width is half of the circle's edge, which is pi times r. So area equals pi r times r — pi r squared.

draw.text: A = pi r × r = pi r²

turns.text: How does matrix multiplication work?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Matrix multiplication combines two matrices into a new one. The key rule: the number of columns in the first must equal the number of rows in the second.

draw.text: Inner dimensions must match: n = n

beats.say: To get each entry in the result, you take one row from the first matrix and one column from the second, multiply matching values, and add them up. It's a dot product.

draw.text: C[ i ][ j ] = row i  .  col j

beats.say: So the entry at row i, column j of the result is the sum over k of A[i][k] times B[k][j]. Each result cell is one row-column pairing.
Because each row of A pairs with every column of B, the shapes multiply out: an m-by-n matrix times an n-by-p matrix gives an m-by-p result.

draw.text: (m x n)  x  (n x p)  =  (m x p)
Not commutative:  A*B rarely equals B*A

beats.say: One more thing: order matters. Matrix multiplication isn't commutative, so A times B usually differs from B times A, and the shapes may not even allow both.

draw.text: Why it matters: transformations, graphics, neural nets

turns.text: Show me a 2 by 2 example.
turns.reply: I'll add a quick 2 by 2 example to the board.

beats.say: Let's take a simple two by two case. A has rows one, two and three, four; B has rows five, six and seven, eight.
For the top-left cell, take row one of A and column one of B: one times five plus two times seven is nineteen.
Top-right: row one of A times column two of B, that's one times six plus two times eight, twenty-two. Then row two gives forty-three and fifty.
So the product is the matrix nineteen, twenty-two, forty-three, fifty. Four dot products, one per cell.

turns.text: How does a neural network learn?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Learning is really just a loop: guess, measure the error, then nudge the settings to be a bit less wrong. Here's the input going in and the output coming out.
Each connection has a weight, a little dial that says how much that signal matters. The network's answer is just all those weighted signals added up and squashed.

draw.text: Each arrow has a weight = a dial we can turn

beats.say: We compare that prediction with the right answer and get a loss, a single number for how wrong we were.
Then the loss flows backwards through the network, and each weight learns its own share of the blame. That's backpropagation.

draw.text: Each weight gets its share of the blame

beats.say: Finally we turn every dial a tiny step in the direction that lowers the loss. Do that thousands of times and the network gets good.

draw.text: Repeat thousands of times = gradient descent

turns.text: More detail on backpropagation.
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Backprop is just the chain rule from calculus, run backwards. Zooming in on one weight: its blame depends on how much the loss changes as that weight moves.

draw.text: blame on w = how loss changes as w changes (chain rule)

beats.say: In the forward pass we save each layer's output. On the way back, the loss's gradient is multiplied by the local slope at each layer, so the number shrinks and moves deeper.

draw.text: Backward: multiply by local slope at each layer

beats.say: That gives us a gradient for every weight in a single sweep, which is what makes deep networks trainable at all. One pass back, one gradient per dial.

draw.text: One backward sweep = a gradient for every weight at once

beats.say: Then we step the other way: subtract a small multiple of the gradient, called the learning rate. Too big and we overshoot, too small and it crawls.

draw.text: new w = w - learning rate x gradient

beats.say: Two things bite in practice: gradients can fade to almost nothing in deep nets, or blow up and destabilise things. That's why we use better activation functions, careful initialisation, and normalisation between layers.

draw.text: Watch out: vanishing or exploding gradients

turns.text: How does a large language model generate text?
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

lesson.title: How a large language model generates text

beats.say: It all starts with your prompt. The model can't read words, so first it chops the text into tokens and turns each one into a list of numbers called an embedding.

Those vectors pass through dozens of stacked transformer layers. Inside each one, attention lets every token look at all the others and decide what's relevant, then a small network refines each token's meaning.
After the last layer, the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary — a probability for what comes next.
It picks one token from that distribution — often the most likely, sometimes with a little randomness for variety. That single new token is the output.
Then the trick: append that token to the input and run the whole thing again. One token at a time, each step feeding the next, until it emits a stop token.

draw.text: Repeat: new token → back into the input

turns.text: What is attention?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Attention is how a token decides which other tokens matter to it. For each token the model builds a query — what am I looking for — and a key and a value for every token it could look at.
It compares its query against every key and scores the match. High scores mean those tokens are relevant — the scores get squashed into weights that add up to one.
Then it takes a weighted blend of the values, so the token's new representation is mostly made of the tokens it found relevant. That's why "it" can pick up that it means "the cat".
Every token does this at once, in parallel, and with several heads at the same time — one head might track grammar, another who-did-what. That's multi-head attention.

draw.text:
Several heads in parallel:
grammar, meaning, long-range links

beats.say: Stack that across all the layers and each token ends up with context from the whole passage — which is what makes the feed-forward net's job so much easier.

turns.text: What is retrieval augmented generation?
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a way of giving a language model outside knowledge at answer time instead of relying only on what it memorised during training.
First the documents are cut into small chunks and turned into vectors, stored in a searchable index. That happens ahead of time.
At question time the same question is embedded, and the index returns the most similar chunks. That is the retrieval step.
Those chunks get pasted into the prompt alongside the question. So the model reads real source text before it answers — that is the augmentation.
The model then generates the answer grounded in that retrieved text, and can cite which chunks it used — which is why RAG cuts down on made-up facts.

turns.text: Where do embeddings come in?
turns.reply: I'll zoom in on the embeddings step.

beats.say: Embeddings appear twice, and it's the same embedding model both times. First it turns each chunk of text into a vector — a long list of numbers that captures meaning.
So a chunk of prose becomes something like this: a few hundred or thousand numbers. Texts with similar meaning end up with similar vectors.
Those vectors are what gets stored in the vector index, so search becomes a nearest-neighbour lookup rather than a keyword match.
Then at question time the question goes through that same model, giving a vector in the same space. Comparing it to the index is exactly what the search arrow does.
The key point: if you embedded chunks with one model and the question with another, the vectors wouldn't be comparable and retrieval would break.

turns.text: Explain how training versus testing data works in machine learning.
turns.reply: I'll sketch it out for you.

beats.say: In machine learning, you split your data into two piles: one the model learns from, and one it's graded on later.
The model studies the training set and adjusts its internal weights to fit those examples. This is where it gets its practice hours.
Then the testing set steps in. The model has never seen these examples, so its score here tells you how it does in the real world.
Why keep them apart? Because a model that just memorizes the training data looks brilliant there but flops on anything new. That's called overfitting.
When you also need to tune settings like parameters or pick between models, carve out a third slice called validation, and keep the test set untouched until the very end.

draw.text: Tune settings here; test set stays sealed

turns.text: What's overfitting?
turns.reply: Let me add that to the board.

beats.say: Overfitting is when a model memorises the training set instead of learning the pattern behind it. It looks amazing on data it has seen, and shaky on anything new.
Watch the two error curves. Training error keeps dropping, but test error comes down, bottoms out, then climbs back up again. That gap opening up is overfitting.
The usual fix is to make the model simpler or stop earlier, plus more data and regularisation. Too simple and it underfits; the balance point is the one that generalises.
To spot and fix overfitting you tune on the validation set, and leave the test set sealed so it stays an honest judge.

draw.text: Test set: only opened at the end

turns.text: Give me a timeline of the space race.
turns.reply: I'll sketch that out for you.

beats.say: The Space Race was a Cold War contest for spaceflight firsts between the Soviet Union and the United States, running roughly from 1957 to 1975. Let me lay it out as a timeline.

It began with Sputnik 1 in October 1957, the first artificial satellite, which stunned the world and started the race in earnest. A month later Sputnik 2 carried Laika, the first living creature in orbit.
The US answered with Explorer 1 in early 1958 and founded NASA that same year. The Soviets then pulled further ahead as Luna 2 hit the Moon in 1959 and Luna 3 photographed its far side.

The big leap came in April 1961, when Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1. The US responded within weeks with Alan Shepard, and Kennedy committed America to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out.

The middle sixties were a build-up. John Glenn orbited in 1962, Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963, and Voskhod 2 saw the first spacewalk in 1965, while the US pulled ahead with Gemini and the giant Saturn V rocket.

The finish line was the Moon. Apollo 8 circled it in December 1968, then on the twentieth of July 1969 Apollo 11 landed Armstrong and Aldrin on the surface, and the US had won the race's headline prize.

After the landing the race wound down. The Soviets moved to space stations with Salyut and Soyuz, NASA flew Skylab, and the two sides finally shook hands in orbit with the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project in 1975.

turns.text: More detail on Apollo 11.

beats.say: Apollo 11 launched on the sixteenth of July 1969 on a Saturn V, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. It took about three days to reach the Moon.

In lunar orbit Collins stayed with the command module Columbia, while Armstrong and Aldrin flew the Eagle lander down to the Sea of Tranquility and touched down on the twentieth of July, with barely twenty seconds of fuel to spare.

Armstrong stepped out first with his famous line about one small step, and Aldrin followed. Between them they spent about two and a half hours on the surface, collecting rock samples and setting up experiments.

draw.text: One small step, 21 Jul; two and a half hours on the surface

beats.say: After docking back with Columbia, they splashed down in the Pacific on the twenty-fourth of July, and the crew spent three weeks in quarantine just in case they had brought something back from the Moon.
